Daily Briefings · Monday, November 16, 2026

Space & Defense Daily — Monday, Nov 16, 2026

ULA's Vulcan failed on its return to flight, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites and grounding half of the Space Force's launch manifest; Starship's upper stage was caught by the tower for the first time, though the booster was lost; Europe will join the next Ukraine talks as an "E5 + EU" team just as Zelensky says the U.S. floated NATO membership in exchange for the Donbas.

← NewerTue, Nov 17, 2026All briefingsOlder →Fri, Nov 13, 2026
NATOEuropean UnionUnited StatesEuropean spaceGlobal space & defense

Top stories: ULA's Vulcan failed about 10 minutes after liftoff on Sunday. It was the company's first total mission failure in 20 years and destroyed 40 Amazon Leo satellites. The rocket is grounded indefinitely, which leaves the Pentagon leaning even harder on SpaceX. SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the launch tower's arms for the first time on Saturday, but the double catch slipped away when the Super Heavy booster aborted and blew up over the Gulf. On Ukraine, Europe will join the next round of talks as an "E5 + EU" team (France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the UK, plus the EU institutions). Meanwhile, Zelensky says U.S. envoys floated NATO membership in exchange for Ukraine leaving the Donbas.

NATO

  • Zelensky says Witkoff and Kushner asked, for the first time, "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" He says that puts NATO "back on the agenda," but Kyiv still won't recognise any seized land, and NATO and Washington haven't commented. Moscow is meanwhile trying to widen the talks into a "new, modern Yalta" on Europe's security order, which Merz rejected. (AFP)
  • Albania's Edi Rama says NATO's planned leaders' summit in Tirana will "for sure not" happen in 2027 and might come in 2028. Allies are considering dropping annual summits, which would avoid a tense meeting with Trump; a NATO official said the next summit will still be in Albania, with no date set. (Al Jazeera)
  • In a reversal, the Pentagon is now expected to cut fewer of its roughly 80,000 troops in Europe than the up to 25,000 allies had feared. Bloomberg's sources point to higher NATO spending and Europe's value as a staging base for the Iran war. (Japan Times / Bloomberg)
  • Estonia will close all road crossings with Russia from Dec. 1. The move follows what its security service says was a GRU-ordered attempt to set fire to and blow up drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn; eight Latvia-based suspects were detained. PM Michal called it part of Russia's "hybrid war against Europe." (POLITICO Europe)
  • Rutte is meeting Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk at NATO headquarters today. (NATO)

European Union

  • Von der Leyen says Europe will "closely engage" in the Russia–Ukraine talks through the E5 + EU format agreed in Dublin on Nov. 13. The EU and Ukraine also agreed steps to speed up membership reforms, and leaders take up Ukraine's 2027 funding at the Nov. 26–27 European Council. (Kyiv Independent)
  • Dublin left the hard questions open: whether Europe names a single envoy (Kallas wants the role but lacks unanimous support) and how to raise at least €45B of Kyiv's roughly €70B gap for 2027. More joint EU borrowing looks increasingly likely. (The Irish Times)
  • The Bundestag budget committee approved a record €139B German defence budget for 2027, up €31.4B. It adds 16 tactical Airbus A400Ms, more MEKO A-200 frigates, and extra money for SATCOM Stage 3 secure satcom and a space-based sensor network. (Aviation Week; hartpunkt)
  • Italy called an FT report that it opposes making Germany a full GCAP partner "entirely misleading." Rome says it proposed observer status only as a fast track to full membership, as Berlin weighs joining after its fighter talks with France collapsed. (Defense News)
  • DG DEFIS published a series of factsheets on European Defence Fund work in sensors, hypersonics, lasers, nanotech and next-gen communications. Highlights include more than €300M for advanced sensing and €68M in the 2026 work programme for countering hypersonic glide vehicles. (European Commission)

United States

  • Vulcan's return to flight (Amazon Leo LV-01) failed about 10 minutes after its 9:40 a.m. PT liftoff on Sunday. Ars reports the problem was in the BE-4-powered booster stage, which overburned and began to spin. Vulcan carries roughly half the Pentagon's national-security launches and was waiting on this flight for recertification, so expect more Space Force missions to move to SpaceX. (Ars Technica; Reuters)
  • Starship Flight 15 reached orbit, deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and the Ship was caught by the tower 22.5 hours after launch, a first. The Super Heavy booster cut its boostback burn short on a low-fuel alarm, aborted the catch and exploded offshore. (The Register)
  • The B-21 Raider made its first weapons release, a conventional weapon dropped in early November from Edwards. The Air Force and Northrop say it moves the bomber into weapons testing, with the first operational aircraft still due at Ellsworth in 2027. (Air & Space Forces Magazine)
  • The Pentagon renamed its Chief Digital and AI Office the "Super Intelligence Office" under Trump's government-wide terminology change. The office keeps the same mission, and Maven and GenAI.mil continue. (Breaking Defense)
  • Senate appropriators put $50M into Commerce's Office of Space Commerce, against an $11M request, keeping the TraCSS civil space-traffic system alive. That eases DoD/Space Force concerns about being stuck warning commercial operators of collisions. (Breaking Defense)
  • LeoLabs bought Massachusetts-based FishEye Software, adding cleared radar and missile-defense engineers as it builds radars for missile warning and tracking. (SpaceNews)
  • Space Launch Delta 45 granted Stoke Space a right of entry to study a second Cape Canaveral pad north of SLC-14, aimed at high-cadence reusable Nova launches. Nova's first orbital flight is targeted for early 2027. (ExterraJSC)

European space

  • The European Parliament's ITRE committee missed its Nov. 10 vote on the EU Space Act, and Nov. 19 is now the likely date. Cybersecurity versus NIS2 and the treatment of non-EU operators are the main splits, the Council has no general approach yet, and final adoption could slip to 2028. (The European Post)
  • Avio says late customer satellites have pushed its third Vega C of 2026, carrying six IRIDE Earth-observation satellites, toward Christmas. It is now pointing to about four launches in 2027. (European Spaceflight)
  • With Vulcan grounded, Ariane 6 becomes more important to Amazon: its fourth Amazon Leo flight is due later this month from Kourou. Arianespace now holds 24 Amazon launches in total. (Ars Technica)

Global space & defense

  • Russia hit at least nine Ukrainian regions overnight Nov. 14–15, and Ukraine struck a refinery and petrochemical plant in Nizhnekamsk, more than 800 km from the front. Zelensky again said Starshield restrictions are letting drones through Ukraine's air defenses. (RFE/RL)
  • Iran's IRGC fired drones at a U.S. base in Bahrain, home of the Fifth Fleet, on Sunday, and Bahrain shot them down. Saudi-backed Yemeni forces pulled back from the Bab el-Mandeb as the Houthis struck Riyadh's airport and the East-West pipeline. (CNBC / Reuters)
  • Reuters reports Trump has told advisers he may hold off on new Iran strikes barring provocations, while keeping the blockade. A third carrier is heading to the region and some U.S. precision-munition stocks are at worrying levels. (Reuters)
  • Rocket Lab flew its 100th mission on Nov. 14, putting a QPS-SAR radar satellite into orbit for Japan's iQPS. Beck says no commercially developed rocket has reached 100 launches faster. (Space.com)
  • China's Shenzhou-23 crew brought in its fourth round of space-radiation exposure samples. One crew member is set to stay aboard Tiangong for a full year. (CGTN)
